blocks.text: O you who nourish the raven in its nest, and repair the broken and crushed jaw of the wild ass. The first part of this distich the Scholiast attributes to David, and explains it thus: الغراب اذا فقس عن فراخه خرجت بيضا فاذا راها ابواها كذلك نفرا عنها فتفتح افواها فيرسل الله تبارك وتعالي لها ذبابا فيدخل في افواها فيركون لها غذا حتي تسود فاذا اسودت عاد ابواها اليها فغذياها ويرفع الله الذباب عنها [al-ghurāb idhā faqasa ʿan firākhihi kharajat bīḍan fa-idhā raʾāhā abawāhā ka-dhālika nafarā ʿanhā fa-taftaḥ afwāhā fa-yursil Allāh tabāraka wa-taʿālī lahā dhubāban fa-yadkhul fī afwāhā fa-yarkūn lahā ghidhā ḥattī taswadd fa-idhā iswaddat ʿāda abawāhā ilayhā fa-ghadhdhayāhā wa-yarfaʿ Allāh al-dhubāb ʿanhā] When the raven hatches its chicks, they come out white. When the parents see them so, they take to flight. But the chicks open their mouths, and God, blessed and exalted, sends them flies, which, entering their mouths, serve them as food until they turn black. Only then do the parents return and feed them, and God removes the flies from them. Alkazuinius teaches the same in words little different. And Damir somewhat more fully: اذا خرجت الفراخ [II, 797] الغراخ من البيض طردتها لانها تخرج قبيحة المنظر حدا انا تكون صغار الاجرام عظيم الروس والمناقر جرد اللون الاجساد متفواتا الاعضا فالابوان [idhā kharajat al-firākh al-ghirākh min al-bayḍ ṭaradathā li-annahā takhruj qabīḥat al-manẓar ḥadā anā takūn ṣighār al-ajrām ʿaẓīm al-rūs wa-al-manāqir jurd al-lawn al-ajsād mutafawwatā al-aʿḍā fa-al-abawān] [col. 206] ينظران الفرخ كذلك فيتركانه فيجعل الله تعالي قوته في الذباب والبعوض الكاين في عشه الي ان يقوي وينبت ريشه فيعود اليه ابواه فيرزقانه [yanẓurān al-farkh ka-dhālika fa-yatrukānih fa-yajʿal Allāh taʿālī qūtah fī al-dhubāb wa-al-baʿūḍ al-kāyin fī ʿushshih ilī an yaqwā wa-yanbut rīshuh fa-yaʿūd ilayh abawāh fa-yarzuqānih] When the chicks come out of the egg, they (the parents) drive them away, because they come out exceedingly ugly to look at. For they have a small body, a large head and beak, a bare appearance, and the limbs of the body disjointed and badly knit together. So the parents, seeing the chick in such a state, desert it. But God most high gives it flies and gnats for food; this food is in the nest until (the chick) gains strength and its feathers grow, and the parents return to it and it is fed by them. To confirm this, another Arab, named Chalpholachmar, describes the foulness of the raven's chicks thus: رايت فرخ الغراب فلم ار صورة اقبح منه ولا اسمج الا اقذر ولا اشر رايت راسا كبيرا ومنقارا طويلا وذلك مع صغر البدن وصغر الجناح وهو امرط نتن الريح [raʾaytu farkh al-ghurāb fa-lam ara ṣūra aqbaḥ minhu wa-lā asmaj al-ā aqdhar wa-lā asharr raʾaytu raʾsan kabīran wa-minqāran ṭawīlan wa-dhālika maʿa ṣighar al-badan wa-ṣighar al-janāḥ wa-huwa amraṭ natin al-rīḥ] I saw a raven's chick, and I have never beheld anything fouler, more misshapen, more unclean or more vile. I saw a large head and a long beak, with a small body and small wings. It was also bare and of fetid breath, etc. There is no time to copy out more from the writings of the Arabs, and these suffice abundantly. So I shall add only this: among the ancient doctors of the church too there were some who embellished this fable in much the same way. Chrysostom, in the Sermon On Elias: Κεχηνότες εἰς ἀέρα τῶν κοράκων οἱ νεοσσοὶ, καὶ παρὰ τῶν γονέων μὴ τρεφόμενοι, ἔχουσιν αὐτοὶ ζῶα μικρά τινα τὴν θείαν ἐπιπέμπουσαν πρόνοιαν διακονούμενα· καὶ οὕτως ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐκεῖνα δεχόμενοι πρὸς αὔξησιν τρέφονται· [Kechēnotes eis aera tōn korakōn hoi neossoi, kai para tōn goneōn mē trephomenoi, echousin autoi zōa mikra tina tēn theian epipempousan pronoian diakonoumena; kai houtōs ek tou aeros ekeina dechomenoi pros auxēsin trephontai] The ravens' chicks, gaping into the air, since they are not fed by their parents, have certain tiny creatures which serve the providence of God, by whom they are sent; and receiving these from the air, they are nourished until they grow up. Olympiodorus on Job: Λέγεται ὁ κόραξ μὴ ἐκτρέφειν τὰ ἔκγονα ὑπὸ λαιμαργίας, ἀλλ᾽ ἀτημελήτους ἐᾶν τοὺς νεοσσούς· τοὺς δὲ, ὑπὸ τῆς ἐνδείας πιεζομένους, φυσικῇ τινι κεχρῆσθαι πρὸς Θεὸν τῇ βοῇ, καὶ ὑπὸ μικρῶν τινων ζωϋφίων, γινομένων ἐν ταῖς νεοσσιαῖς, ἐκτρέφεσθαι. [Legetai ho korax mē ektrephein ta ekgona hypo laimargias, all᾽ atēmelētous ean tous neossous; tous de, hypo tēs endeias piezomenous, physikē tini kechrēsthai pros Theon tē boē, kai hypo mikrōn tinōn zōyphiōn, ginomenōn en tais neossiais, ektrephesthai] The raven is said, out of gluttony, not to rear its offspring, but to abandon its chicks uncared for; and they, pressed by hunger, use a kind of natural cry to God, and are nourished by certain small creatures which are born in the nests. Gregory on Job, book 30: When its chicks are hatched (the raven), as is reported, neglects to provide them food before they turn black by growing feathers, and lets them suffer hunger [II, 798] until its own likeness is seen in them through the blackness of their feathers. They wander here and there in the nest and seek the help of food with open mouth. But when they have begun to turn black, it seeks the food to be given them all the more eagerly, the longer it has put off feeding them. Isidore, Etymologies book 12, ch. 7: This bird is said [col. 207] not to give its hatched chicks full food until it recognizes in them the blackness of the feathers, the likeness of its own colour. But after it has seen them foul (I would prefer black) with feathers, having recognized them wholly, it feeds them more abundantly. Cassiodorus on the Psalms, and the author who circulates under the name of Jerome, say that the chicks, thus neglected, are fed by heavenly dew, which is the food of cicadas, not of ravens. But who would believe that flies and gnats are born in a raven's nest in such abundance as to suffice to feed several chicks, and very greedy ones at that? And that the gnats, as soon as they are born, of their own accord thrust themselves into the chicks' mouths to be devoured? Or that the parents hate their chicks because they are born partly featherless, when the very same thing happens to other birds? Or that, having once deserted them, they return to them as soon as they are clothed with feathers, or when these are blacker, as if someone had told them that their chicks are now in better shape and there is no longer reason to shrink from them? In a word, this is certain and already a common saying: to no bird is its own nest foul; and there is no animal that is not pleased by the form of its like. Hence Epicharmus in Laertius, in the Life of Plato:
— — — Καὶ γὰρ ὁ κύων κυνὶ Κάλλιστον εἶναι φαίνεται, καὶ βοῦς βοΐ, ῎Ονος δ᾽ ὄνῳ κάλλιστον, ὗς δ᾽ ὑΐ· [Kai gar ho kyōn kyni kalliston einai phainetai, kai bous boi, onos d᾽ onō kalliston, hys d᾽ hyi]
